doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: How the Cookers began from Night of the Cookers and Freddie Hubbard
summary: Weiss explains that his eight years with Freddie Hubbard led to a Night of the Cookers reunion that grew into the Cookers, and that he sees himself as coordinator rather than leader of older masters.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I understand the group came out of a Freddie Hubbard connection. But I wonder if at some point, did you feel not — intimidated isn’t the right word. Was it a bit odd for you to be the head of a group where the majority of the players were anywhere from twenty to almost thirty years older than you? Now you had established yourself certainly as a presence in New York and had your due respect. But still, I’m wondering if any of this has been odd for you to sort of be in charge of musicians of that pedigree?

Well there’s many things I could say about that. I did work with Freddie Hubbard for eight years before — I guess they kind of overlapped a little bit. And the first night of the Cookers gig, or the first attempt at it, was something they asked me to put together because of my connection with Freddie. The guy wanted Freddie to come and like be the emcee, you know. The Night of the Cookers concert I don’t remember the exact dates, but they are right around Freddie’s birthday, and there was this club in Brooklyn where the guy’s first concert when he was a kid was the Night of the Cookers concert. So he was always enamored with it. And every year he would try to do something, like try to get Freddie to come in. But Freddie lived in California. And he didn’t have a very big club, so it was kind of a challenge to get Freddie to come in to blow out some birthday cake. And one year he finally said like, “I want to put together a Night of the Cookers reunion. I want Freddie to come but I want all the other guys there.” So we got Pete La Roca and James Spaulding. We tried to get Harold Mabern but he wasn’t available. Larry Ridley did it. And when Mabern couldn’t do it we decided I could put together

some more Freddie Hubbard alumni. Ronnie Mathews did it and Kiane Zawadi did it. And that concert was a success. And Pete La Roca and James Spaulding were great. And that’s what started it. It morphed into what the Cookers are today, but it started as this Night of the Cookers celebration, that people reached out to me because at the time I was working with Freddie, and, you know, they thought I can help get them to do something Freddie didn’t really want to do which was come fly to New York to blow out a birthday cake. So as far — I don’t consider myself the leader. That’s one thing. I mean I try to get the gigs, I coordinate stuff, I’m on the trumpet. But in the rehearsal it’s not like, “Look Billy, you’re going to have to —” I mean there is maybe a little bit of a straw boss thing where I’m, like okay let’s play this tune. Okay well that didn’t really sound right, “Let’s try that again.” It’s never like, “You really need to —” and those guys know it. I mean they’ll mess with me sometimes. Billy Hart very early on was like, “Look man, we just don’t do this for anybody.” You know? I mean and their elders did that to them. This thing was always like look, this is a small club and we don’t let just anybody — and you can’t just walk in here and do this, you’ve got to bring something to the table. And I’ve always felt that pressure. You know I started on jazz late. So I always felt I was behind the curve. I always felt I was trying to catch up with everybody. And this in a way is putting me in a situation where I’m still doing that.
